input: The rate constant k of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures in order to characterise the way in which the rate of the reaction responds to temperature. At 300 K, the rate constant k was found to be 0.017 s-1, whereas at 340 K it had increased very markedly to 0.642 s-1, which represents an increase by a factor of 37.8 across the interval studied. It should be noted that this second value was not measured directly but was computed from the Arrhenius relation using an activation energy of 77 kJ mol-1, and it is therefore presented as a derived value rather than as a direct experimental measurement. Each of the temperatures was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of k was 4%, which indicates a good level of repeatability in the underlying measurements. It should also be borne in mind, however, that above 340 K the solvent was found to evaporate during sampling, which meant that no rate constant is reported above that temperature, and the temperature range over which data are available is therefore limited accordingly. The distinction between the measured and the derived values is worth keeping in mind, since the derived value depends not only on the measurements made at the lower temperature but also on the extent to which the Arrhenius relation, with a single activation energy, faithfully describes the reaction over the whole interval.
target: The rate constant $k$ of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, $k$ = 0.017 s-1. At 340 K, $k$ = 0.642 s-1, a factor of 37.8 above the lower-temperature value. The second value is derived, not measured: it was computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 77 kJ mol-1, and it carries the assumptions of that relation with it. The relation treats the activation energy as constant over the interval, and the derived value is exact only to the extent that the reaction keeps the same mechanism, and the same energy barrier, across the whole range. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of $k$ was 4%. The spread therefore describes the repeatability of the measurement at each temperature; it does not extend to the derived value, whose uncertainty also includes whatever error the Arrhenius extrapolation contributes. Triplicate measurement at each temperature is what allows that spread to be stated at all: a single measurement would have given a value with no measure of its own scatter. The temperature range of the study is bounded by the solvent: above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, and no rate constant is reported above that temperature. The two values as they stand show a strong temperature dependence over the interval measured, with the upper value resting on the Arrhenius computation rather than on a sampling measurement of the same standing as the lower one. A measured upper value, taken under sampling that prevents the evaporation, would put the derived figure to the test.
